scope.top_bubble: Classical mechanics from Newtonian foundations through Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations

nodes.title: Basic Calculus
nodes.one_liner: Differentiation and integration of single-variable functions
outcomes: Compute derivatives using standard rules
Evaluate definite and indefinite integrals
Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus

nodes.title: Vector Algebra
nodes.one_liner: Vector operations including dot product, cross product, and component decomposition
outcomes: Perform dot and cross products
Decompose vectors into components
Apply vector identities to physical problems

nodes.title: Coordinate Systems
nodes.one_liner: Polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinate systems with basis vectors and transformations
outcomes: Convert between Cartesian and curvilinear coordinates
Express velocity and acceleration in polar coordinates
Write area and volume elements in each system

nodes.title: Ordinary Differential Equations
nodes.one_liner: Solution methods for first- and second-order linear ODEs with constant coefficients
outcomes: Solve first-order separable and linear ODEs
Solve second-order constant-coefficient ODEs
Identify general vs particular solutions

nodes.title: Partial Derivatives
nodes.one_liner: Differentiation of multivariable functions and the multivariable chain rule
outcomes: Compute partial derivatives of multivariable functions
Apply the multivariable chain rule
Find total differentials

nodes.title: Linear Algebra Basics
nodes.one_liner: Matrices, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and diagonalisation
outcomes: Multiply matrices and find determinants
Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors
Diagonalise symmetric matrices

nodes.title: Multiple Integrals
nodes.one_liner: Double and triple integrals with change of variables
outcomes: Evaluate double integrals over regions
Apply the Jacobian for coordinate changes
Compute triple integrals in cylindrical and spherical coordinates

nodes.title: Taylor Series
nodes.one_liner: Power series expansion of functions about a point
outcomes: Expand functions as Taylor series
Determine radius of convergence
Use Taylor expansion to approximate functions near equilibrium

nodes.title: Fourier Series
nodes.one_liner: Decomposition of periodic functions into sinusoidal components
outcomes: Compute Fourier coefficients
Represent a periodic driving force as a sum of harmonics
Apply Parseval's theorem

nodes.title: Calculus of Variations
nodes.one_liner: Finding functions that extremise functionals defined as integrals
outcomes: Define a functional and state the extremisation problem
Derive the Euler-Lagrange equation for a general functional
Solve the brachistochrone and catenary problems

nodes.title: Legendre Transform
nodes.one_liner: Transformation replacing a function of one variable with a function of its conjugate variable
outcomes: Define the Legendre transform and its inverse
Apply it to convert between Lagrangian and Hamiltonian
Identify conjugate variable pairs

nodes.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
nodes.one_liner: The three foundational laws relating force, mass, and acceleration
outcomes: State and apply Newton's three laws
Draw free-body diagrams and solve force-balance problems
Identify action-reaction pairs

nodes.title: Momentum and Impulse
nodes.one_liner: Linear momentum conservation and the impulse-momentum theorem
outcomes: Apply conservation of momentum to collisions
Calculate impulse from force-time profiles
Distinguish elastic from inelastic collisions

nodes.title: Friction and Contact Forces
nodes.one_liner: Static and kinetic friction, normal forces, and constraint forces
outcomes: Apply Coulomb friction model
Solve inclined-plane and pulley problems
Identify when static friction transitions to kinetic

nodes.title: Circular Motion
nodes.one_liner: Uniform and non-uniform motion along circular paths
outcomes: Derive centripetal acceleration
Apply Newton's second law in radial-tangential coordinates
Solve banked-curve and conical-pendulum problems

nodes.title: Work-Energy Theorem
nodes.one_liner: Net work equals change in kinetic energy
outcomes: Derive the work-energy theorem from Newton's second law
Calculate work done by variable forces via integration
Apply the theorem to multi-step mechanical problems

nodes.title: Potential Energy
nodes.one_liner: Energy stored in configuration, defined for conservative forces
outcomes: Define potential energy as negative work done by a conservative force
Derive gravitational and elastic potential energy
Sketch and interpret potential energy curves

nodes.title: Conservative Forces
nodes.one_liner: Forces whose work is path-independent, expressible as gradients of scalar potentials
outcomes: Test whether a force is conservative via the curl condition
Derive force from a potential energy function
Identify non-conservative forces and their effects on energy budgets

nodes.title: Energy Conservation
nodes.one_liner: Total mechanical energy is constant when only conservative forces act
outcomes: Derive conservation of energy from the work-energy theorem
Solve problems using energy methods instead of force methods
Identify when energy conservation applies and when it does not

nodes.title: Centre of Mass
nodes.one_liner: Mass-weighted average position and its role in multi-body dynamics
outcomes: Compute the centre of mass of discrete and continuous distributions
Apply the centre-of-mass equation of motion
Separate internal and external forces in multi-body systems

nodes.title: Reference Frames
nodes.one_liner: Inertial frames, Galilean transformations, and the principle of relativity
outcomes: Distinguish inertial from non-inertial frames
Apply Galilean velocity and acceleration transformations
State Newton's laws in different inertial frames

nodes.title: Non-Inertial Frames
nodes.one_liner: Fictitious forces arising in accelerating reference frames
outcomes: Derive the equation of motion in a linearly accelerating frame
Identify centrifugal and Coriolis terms
Solve problems in the accelerating-elevator frame

nodes.title: Rotating Reference Frames
nodes.one_liner: Kinematics and dynamics in frames rotating with constant angular velocity
outcomes: Derive the five-term acceleration formula in a rotating frame
Identify centrifugal and Coriolis pseudo-forces
Transform equations of motion between rotating and inertial frames

nodes.title: Coriolis Force
nodes.one_liner: Velocity-dependent fictitious force deflecting motion in rotating frames
outcomes: Derive the Coriolis acceleration for motion on Earth's surface
Explain Foucault pendulum deflection
Calculate trajectory deflection of a projectile due to Earth's rotation

nodes.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
nodes.one_liner: Oscillatory motion about a stable equilibrium under a linear restoring force
outcomes: Derive the SHM equation from Hooke's law
Express solutions in terms of amplitude, frequency, and phase
Relate SHM to energy oscillation between kinetic and potential

nodes.title: Damped Oscillations
nodes.one_liner: Oscillatory motion with energy dissipation via a velocity-dependent drag force
outcomes: Solve the damped-oscillator ODE for under-, critically-, and over-damped cases
Define the quality factor Q
Sketch the amplitude envelope for each damping regime

nodes.title: Driven Oscillations and Resonance
nodes.one_liner: Steady-state response of a damped oscillator to a periodic driving force
outcomes: Derive the steady-state amplitude and phase as functions of driving frequency
Locate the resonance peak and its width in terms of Q
Decompose a general periodic drive into Fourier components

nodes.title: Coupled Oscillations
nodes.one_liner: Two or more oscillators linked by coupling forces
outcomes: Set up the coupled equations of motion in matrix form
Find normal-mode frequencies from the eigenvalue problem
Express general motion as a superposition of normal modes

nodes.title: Normal Modes
nodes.one_liner: Collective oscillation patterns in which all parts move at the same frequency
outcomes: Define normal modes and normal coordinates
Diagonalise the mass-and-spring matrix to find mode frequencies
Relate initial conditions to mode amplitudes

nodes.title: Stability of Equilibria
nodes.one_liner: Classifying equilibrium points as stable, unstable, or neutral via the potential energy curvature
outcomes: Find equilibrium points from dV/dx = 0
Classify stability from the sign of d²V/dx²
Linearise the equation of motion near a stable equilibrium to obtain SHM

nodes.title: Angular Velocity and Acceleration
nodes.one_liner: Rotational kinematics: angular displacement, velocity, and acceleration as vectors
outcomes: Define angular velocity as a vector along the rotation axis
Relate linear and angular velocity via v = ω × r
Apply rotational kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration

nodes.title: Torque
nodes.one_liner: Rotational analogue of force: τ = r × F
outcomes: Compute torque from force and lever arm
Apply the rotational form of Newton's second law τ = Iα
Solve static-equilibrium problems with torques

nodes.title: Moment of Inertia
nodes.one_liner: Resistance to angular acceleration, depending on mass distribution relative to the rotation axis
outcomes: Compute moments of inertia for simple bodies by integration
Use the parallel-axis and perpendicular-axis theorems
Relate moment of inertia to rotational kinetic energy

nodes.title: Parallel Axis Theorem
nodes.one_liner: Relating the moment of inertia about any axis to that about the centre-of-mass axis
outcomes: State and prove the parallel-axis theorem
Apply it to compute moments about displaced axes
Use the perpendicular-axis theorem for planar bodies

nodes.title: Angular Momentum
nodes.one_liner: Rotational analogue of linear momentum: L = r × p = Iω
outcomes: Compute angular momentum for point particles and rigid bodies
Apply conservation of angular momentum when net torque is zero
Analyse variable-inertia systems like spinning ice skaters

nodes.title: Rigid Body Rotation
nodes.one_liner: Combined translational and rotational motion of extended rigid bodies
outcomes: Apply Newton's second law for rotation and translation simultaneously
Solve rolling-without-slipping problems
Use energy methods for combined translation and rotation

nodes.title: Precession and Gyroscopes
nodes.one_liner: Torque-induced precession of spinning bodies and gyroscopic stability
outcomes: Derive the precession rate of a spinning top under gravity
Explain gyroscopic stability qualitatively and quantitatively
Analyse nutation as a perturbation on steady precession

nodes.title: Gravitational Force
nodes.one_liner: Newton's law of universal gravitation and gravitational potential energy
outcomes: State Newton's law of gravitation
Derive gravitational potential energy
Apply the shell theorem for spherically symmetric bodies

nodes.title: Reduced Mass
nodes.one_liner: Transforming a two-body problem into an equivalent one-body problem
outcomes: Derive the reduced mass μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂)
Separate centre-of-mass and relative coordinates
Rewrite the two-body equation of motion as a one-body problem

nodes.title: Two-Body Central Force Problem
nodes.one_liner: Complete solution of two bodies interacting via a central force
outcomes: Reduce the two-body problem using centre-of-mass and relative coordinates
Identify conserved quantities (energy, angular momentum)
Classify orbits by energy and angular momentum

nodes.title: Effective Potential
nodes.one_liner: Reducing the radial equation of motion to a one-dimensional energy problem
outcomes: Derive the effective potential including the centrifugal barrier
Sketch V_eff(r) and identify turning points
Classify bound and unbound orbits from V_eff

nodes.title: Orbit Equation
nodes.one_liner: Deriving the shape of orbits under a central force using the Binet equation
outcomes: Derive the orbit equation r(θ) for an inverse-square force
Identify conic sections from the eccentricity
Relate orbital parameters to energy and angular momentum

nodes.title: Kepler's Laws and Orbits
nodes.one_liner: Elliptical orbits, equal areas, and the period-semimajor axis relation
outcomes: Derive all three of Kepler's laws from Newton's gravitation
Calculate orbital period and velocity for elliptical orbits
Apply Kepler's third law to planetary and satellite motion

nodes.title: Scattering and Cross Sections
nodes.one_liner: Deflection of particles by a central force and the concept of differential cross section
outcomes: Define impact parameter and scattering angle
Derive the Rutherford scattering cross section
Relate differential cross section to deflection function

nodes.title: Constraints and Degrees of Freedom
nodes.one_liner: How holonomic and non-holonomic constraints reduce the configuration space
outcomes: Classify holonomic and non-holonomic constraints
Count degrees of freedom for a constrained system
Express constraints as equations relating coordinates

nodes.title: Generalized Coordinates
nodes.one_liner: Choosing coordinates that naturally respect constraints
outcomes: Select generalized coordinates for a given constrained system
Express kinetic and potential energy in generalized coordinates
Relate generalized coordinates to Cartesian positions via transformation equations

nodes.title: Virtual Work and Virtual Displacements
nodes.one_liner: Work done by forces through infinitesimal displacements consistent with constraints
outcomes: Define virtual displacement as an infinitesimal displacement consistent with constraints at fixed time
State the principle of virtual work for static equilibrium
Apply virtual work to derive equilibrium conditions without solving for constraint forces

nodes.title: D'Alembert's Principle
nodes.one_liner: Extending virtual work to dynamics by treating inertial forces as applied forces
outcomes: State D'Alembert's principle: (F - ma) · δr = 0
Derive equations of motion without constraint forces
Show that D'Alembert's principle leads to the Euler-Lagrange equations

nodes.title: Principle of Least Action
nodes.one_liner: The physical trajectory extremises the action integral S = ∫L dt
outcomes: Define the action functional and state Hamilton's principle
Show that δS = 0 yields the Euler-Lagrange equations
Understand the relationship between least action and energy conservation

nodes.title: Euler-Lagrange Equation
nodes.one_liner: The fundamental equation of Lagrangian mechanics: d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) - ∂L/∂q = 0
outcomes: Derive the Euler-Lagrange equation from the action principle
Apply it to obtain equations of motion for mechanical systems
Identify the connection to Newton's second law for simple cases

nodes.title: Lagrangian Mechanics
nodes.one_liner: Complete reformulation of classical mechanics using L = T - V and the Euler-Lagrange equations
outcomes: Construct the Lagrangian for multi-degree-of-freedom systems
Derive and solve the equations of motion for constrained systems
Compare Lagrangian and Newtonian approaches for the same problem

nodes.title: Symmetries and Noether's Theorem
nodes.one_liner: Every continuous symmetry of the Lagrangian yields a conserved quantity
outcomes: State Noether's theorem and identify the conserved quantity for a given symmetry
Derive conservation of momentum from translational symmetry
Derive conservation of angular momentum from rotational symmetry

nodes.title: Cyclic Coordinates and Conserved Momenta
nodes.one_liner: Coordinates absent from the Lagrangian whose conjugate momenta are conserved
outcomes: Identify cyclic coordinates by inspection of the Lagrangian
Derive the conserved conjugate momentum for each cyclic coordinate
Use cyclic coordinates to reduce the order of the equations of motion

nodes.title: Lagrange Multipliers for Constraints
nodes.one_liner: Incorporating non-eliminable constraints into the Lagrangian formalism
outcomes: Augment the Lagrangian with constraint terms and multipliers
Solve the augmented Euler-Lagrange equations for motion and constraint forces
Identify when multipliers are preferable to eliminating coordinates

nodes.title: Small Oscillations (Lagrangian Treatment)
nodes.one_liner: Systematic Lagrangian analysis of small oscillations about equilibrium for multi-DOF systems
outcomes: Taylor-expand the Lagrangian to quadratic order about equilibrium
Set up the T and V matrices and solve the generalised eigenvalue problem
Find normal-mode frequencies and mode shapes for multi-DOF systems

nodes.title: The Hamiltonian
nodes.one_liner: Legendre transform of the Lagrangian: H(q, p, t) = Σpᵢq̇ᵢ - L
outcomes: Construct the Hamiltonian from the Lagrangian via Legendre transform
Identify when H equals total energy and when it does not
Express the Hamiltonian for standard mechanical systems

nodes.title: Hamilton's Equations of Motion
nodes.one_liner: First-order equations q̇ = ∂H/∂p, ṗ = -∂H/∂q replacing the second-order Euler-Lagrange equation
outcomes: Derive Hamilton's equations from the Hamiltonian
Solve Hamilton's equations for simple systems
Compare the structure of Hamiltonian and Lagrangian equations

nodes.title: Phase Space
nodes.one_liner: The 2n-dimensional space of generalised coordinates and momenta
outcomes: Plot phase portraits for one-dimensional systems
State and apply Liouville's theorem on phase-space volume conservation
Identify fixed points and classify their stability from the phase portrait

nodes.title: Poisson Brackets
nodes.one_liner: Algebraic structure encoding the time evolution and symmetries of Hamiltonian systems
outcomes: Define the Poisson bracket {f, g}
Express time evolution as df/dt = {f, H} + ∂f/∂t
Verify the fundamental Poisson brackets {qᵢ, pⱼ} = δᵢⱼ

Partial differentiation extends single-variable calculus to multiple variables
Multiple integrals extend single-variable integration to higher dimensions

Computing Fourier coefficients requires integration
Understanding series representations of functions provides the conceptual basis for Fourier decomposition
Deriving the Euler-Lagrange equation from a functional requires partial differentiation of the integrand
Functionals are defined as integrals; their evaluation and manipulation require integration techniques
The Legendre transform is defined through partial derivatives of the original function
Understanding convexity and the geometric interpretation requires single-variable calculus
Forces and accelerations are vectors; Newton's second law is a vector equation
Acceleration is the second derivative of position; applying Newton's laws requires differentiation and integration
Momentum conservation follows from Newton's third law; impulse is the integral of Newton's second law
Solving friction problems requires applying Newton's second law with constraint and friction forces
Damping forces are friction/drag forces opposing motion; the damped oscillator models their effect on periodic systems
Centripetal acceleration requires a net inward force governed by Newton's second law
Resolving forces into radial and tangential components requires vector decomposition
The work-energy theorem is derived by integrating Newton's second law along the path
Work is defined as an integral of force over displacement
Potential energy is defined as negative work done by conservative forces, which requires the work concept
Conservative forces are defined as those derivable from a potential energy function
The curl condition for conservative forces requires vector calculus operations
Conservative forces are defined by path-independence of work done
The curl condition ∇×F=0 requires evaluation in appropriate coordinate systems
Mechanical energy conservation holds only for conservative force systems
Conservation of energy equates the sum of kinetic and potential energy to a constant
Energy conservation is derived by applying the work-energy theorem to conservative forces
The centre-of-mass equation of motion follows from summing Newton's second law over all particles
Computing the centre of mass of continuous bodies requires integration over the mass distribution
The concept of inertial frames is defined by the validity of Newton's laws
Non-inertial frames are defined in contrast to inertial frames
Rotating frames are a specific class of non-inertial frames with angular velocity
The centrifugal and Coriolis terms arise from the kinematics of rotation
The five-term acceleration formula requires cross products and vector decomposition
The Coriolis force is derived within the rotating-frame formalism
The SHM equation is Newton's second law applied to a linear restoring force
The SHM equation ẍ + ω²x = 0 is a second-order ODE requiring standard solution methods
SHM involves continuous exchange between kinetic and potential energy at constant total energy
Damped oscillation extends SHM by adding a dissipative term
The damped oscillator equation is a second-order ODE with characteristic equation analysis
Driven oscillations build on the damped oscillator by adding a periodic driving force
A general periodic driving force is decomposed into Fourier harmonics, each analysed independently
Coupled oscillations generalise SHM to multiple interacting oscillators
The coupled equations of motion are written as a matrix eigenvalue problem
Normal modes are the eigenvectors of the coupled-oscillation matrix
Finding normal modes requires diagonalising the stiffness matrix
Stability is classified by the curvature of the potential energy at equilibrium
Linearisation near equilibrium uses a Taylor expansion of the potential to quadratic order
Angular velocity generalises the kinematics of circular motion to arbitrary rotation
Angular velocity is a pseudo-vector requiring cross-product formalism (v = ω × r)
Torque is derived from Newton's second law applied to rotational motion
The rotational equation τ = Iα requires the concept of angular acceleration
Computing moments of inertia for continuous bodies requires integration over the mass distribution
Moment of inertia relates angular velocity to rotational kinetic energy and angular momentum
The parallel-axis theorem transforms a known centre-of-mass moment to a displaced axis
The time derivative of angular momentum equals the net torque
Angular momentum L = r × p extends the concept of linear momentum to rotation
Rigid-body dynamics requires computing moments of inertia about various axes
Rolling and spinning problems require conservation and computation of angular momentum
Rigid-body equations of motion equate net torque to the rate of change of angular momentum
Precession arises from torque changing the direction of the angular momentum vector
Gravitational torque on a spinning top drives its precession
Gyroscopic motion involves a rapidly spinning rigid body
Newton's law of gravitation is stated alongside and applied through Newton's laws of motion
Gravitational problems with spherical symmetry require spherical coordinates and the shell theorem
The reduced-mass transformation uses centre-of-mass and relative coordinates
Deriving the reduced-mass equation of motion applies Newton's second law to each body
The two-body problem is solved by reducing to an equivalent one-body problem via reduced mass
Central force motion conserves angular momentum, confining the orbit to a plane
The radial equation of motion uses the effective potential to classify orbit types
Energy conservation determines whether orbits are bound or unbound
Solving the equation of motion requires integrating a second-order ODE in the radial coordinate
The effective potential is derived by writing the total energy in radial form using conservation of energy
The centrifugal barrier L²/2μr² in V_eff arises from conservation of angular momentum
Decomposing motion into radial and angular parts requires polar or spherical coordinates
The orbit equation is derived from the effective-potential energy equation
Solving for r(θ) requires solving a second-order ODE (the Binet equation)
Kepler's laws follow from the orbit equation with an inverse-square force
Kepler orbits are the specific case of the orbit equation under Newtonian gravity
Scattering trajectories are analysed using the effective potential for unbound orbits
Cross-section calculations require solid angle integration in spherical coordinates
Constraint forces supplement Newton's laws; counting DOF determines the number of independent equations
Constraints are expressed as equations relating coordinate variables
Generalized coordinates are chosen to automatically satisfy holonomic constraints
Constructing generalized coordinates requires facility with coordinate transformations
Virtual work extends the concept of mechanical work from Newton's framework to constrained systems
Virtual displacements must be consistent with constraints at fixed time
D'Alembert's principle generalises virtual work from statics to dynamics
D'Alembert's principle treats ma as a fictitious force applied within Newton's framework
Hamilton's principle extremises the action functional, which is a variational problem
The Lagrangian L = T - V encodes the energy structure; conservation of energy follows from time-translation symmetry of the action
The Euler-Lagrange equation is the variational equation for the action functional
The equation involves partial derivatives ∂L/∂q and ∂L/∂q̇ of the Lagrangian
The Euler-Lagrange equation is the central computational tool of the Lagrangian formulation
The Lagrangian is expressed in generalized coordinates; cannot formulate problems without them
The variational principle provides the theoretical foundation for the entire formulation
D'Alembert's principle provides the physical bridge from Newtonian to Lagrangian mechanics
The Lagrangian L = T - V is defined in terms of kinetic and potential energy
Noether's theorem applies to symmetries of the Lagrangian
The proof of Noether's theorem uses variational calculus
Cyclic coordinates are identified from the structure of the Lagrangian
A coordinate is cyclic when ∂L/∂q = 0, requiring partial differentiation
Lagrange multipliers augment the standard Lagrangian formalism for non-eliminable constraints
Multipliers handle constraints that cannot be eliminated by coordinate choice
The Lagrangian treatment of small oscillations constructs T and V matrices from the Lagrangian
Small oscillations are defined about a stable equilibrium point
The T and V matrices come from Taylor-expanding the Lagrangian to quadratic order
Normal-mode frequencies are eigenvalues of the generalised eigenvalue problem Vx = ω²Tx
The Lagrangian treatment provides the systematic framework for finding normal modes of multi-DOF systems
The Hamiltonian is derived from the Lagrangian via Legendre transform
The Hamiltonian H = Σpᵢq̇ᵢ - L is the Legendre transform of L with respect to q̇
Hamilton's equations are derived from the Hamiltonian
Hamilton's equations q̇ = ∂H/∂p, ṗ = -∂H/∂q are partial derivatives of H
Phase-space trajectories are the solutions of Hamilton's equations
Phase space is a 2n-dimensional coordinate space requiring facility with higher-dimensional coordinate concepts
Poisson brackets encode the algebraic structure of Hamilton's equations
The Poisson bracket {f,g} is defined as a sum of partial derivatives
